idiom_name: settings attribute from os.environ, injected callable; django-waffle inside Django
implementation_notes: The router is a settings attribute or a module-level parsed dict: os.environ.get('FF_NEW_CHECKOUT') is read once at start-up into a settings object, and the toggle point is `if settings.new_checkout:` - which keeps the flag greppable and cheap. Parse the string honestly (lower() in {'1','true','yes'}) because any non-empty environment value is truthy, and inject a callable or a small FeatureFlags object into the code under test instead of letting library code read the environment, so both branches are exercised with a stub. Django projects get the full structure from django-waffle (flag_is_active(request, name) with everyone/percent/user/group criteria and a database-backed Flag model), which is where a context-aware router with rollout semantics is still justified.
pitfalls: Module-level flags are fixed at import time, and a long-lived worker (gunicorn, Celery) keeps the old value for its whole life; use a callable or a settings refresh when the flip must be observed.
Reading os.environ inside a function couples the code to the process environment and defeats monkeypatching in tests; pass the flag in.
Any non-empty string is truthy in Python, so os.environ.get(name) alone turns 'false' into an enabled feature.
Threading and forking aside, a plain module attribute is not a sync point: if one thread rewrites the settings object while another reads it, both branches can execute in one request.
